entities.summary:
Charlottenburg Palace, a magnificent example of Baroque architecture, was commissioned in 1695 by Friedrich I of Prussia as a summer residence for his wife, Sophie Charlotte. Located in Berlin, Germany, this palace became a symbol of the rising power of Prussia during the Early Modern period. Its construction reflects the broader cultural and artistic movements of the time, particularly the influence of French architecture and the aspirations of the Prussian monarchy to align itself with the cultural elite of Europe.

The palace witnessed significant developments over the years, particularly under the reign of Frederick the Great, who expanded it extensively from 1740 to 1786. The addition of the New Wing in 1781, designed by architect Georg Friedrich Knobelsdorff, transformed Charlottenburg into a grandiose residence, featuring opulent rooms and lavish gardens. The palace served not only as a royal residence but also as a venue for important political and cultural events, reflecting the evolving identity and ambitions of Prussia.

The legacy of Charlottenburg Palace extends beyond its architectural significance; it became a national symbol of German history and culture. Following the unification of Germany in 1871, the palace was further restored and repurposed, becoming a museum that showcases Prussian art and history. Today, it stands as a testament to the grandeur of the Prussian monarchy and the cultural developments of the Early Modern period, attracting millions of visitors annually.

'As a royal residence, Charlottenburg Palace encapsulates the ambitions and transformations of Prussia, embodying both the artistic and political aspirations of its time.' The palace's gardens, designed in the French style, remain a key feature, representing the intersection of nature and royal power that characterized European royal estates.
